h1:
Khao Soi & Nam Ngiao in Mae Hong Son
10 Spots Locals Actually Eat At
intro: Mae Hong Son does khao soi and nam ngiao a little differently from Chiang Mai. Here the khao soi broth is mellow and rounded, not fiery, while nam ngiao comes as a Shan-style dish, pale orange from tomatoes and kapok flowers, and milder than the Chiang Rai version. We pulled together the shops people in Mae Hong Son actually eat at, drawing on reviews and long-running spots, and we tell you the area, the price, and what stands out — straight up.

blocks.html: If you come to Mae Hong Son and want to eat something genuinely local, khao soi and nam ngiao are the two dishes to try. What sets them apart here are their Shan roots: the broth doesn't lean into heat the way it does elsewhere in the north, but instead plays up fragrant spice and a rounded, balanced flavor that's easy for everyone from kids to grandparents. We've ordered the shops by how often locals bring them up and how long they've been around, working from in-town spots out toward Pai and Ban Rak Thai.

blocks.text: How Mae Hong Son khao soi and nam ngiao differ from elsewhere

items: The khao soi isn't fiery — the coconut-curry broth uses Shan curry paste and comes out mellow rather than hot, so it's easy going even if you're not a spice fan.
Nam ngiao is a clear broth — the Shan style is pale orange from tomatoes and kapok flowers, milder than Chiang Rai nam ngiao, with plenty of crispy fried noodles on top.
Eaten with fried sides — locals like to order crispy snacks such as Shan-style fried chickpea fritters (khang pong) or fried tofu to go with it, dipped in roasted dried chili.
Breakfast is prime time — many of the famous shops open from morning to early afternoon and sell out for good, so showing up late means risking missing out.

blocks.text: 10 khao soi & nam ngiao spots locals actually eat at

items.name: Pa Nuan Khao Soi
items.blurb: The legendary khao soi shop of Mae Hong Son, open for over 60 years. The broth is mellow and balanced rather than fiery, and you can pick chicken, beef or pork — plus the stir-fried khao soi that's the shop's signature. The room has an old-school feel and the owner is warm. This is the one spot locals and visitors agree you have to hit.
items.meta: Off Phadung Muay Tor Rd, Chong Kham · Open 08:00–16:30 daily

items.name: Khao Soi Ban Suan Pa Nuan (Branch 2)
items.blurb: Pa Nuan's second location, set up as a garden shop with comfier seating than the original. Same khao soi recipe. A good call if the first branch is packed or you'd rather linger over a coffee afterward.
items.meta: In Mae Hong Son town · Open daytime

items.name: Khanom Jeen Nam Ngiao, Sai Yud Market
items.blurb: A century-old morning market in the middle of town with a stall serving proper Shan-style khanom jeen nam ngiao — broth fragrant with turmeric and tomato, a heavy scatter of crispy fried noodles, eaten with warm tofu and blanched winged beans. It's a breakfast locals genuinely eat, and the price is easy.
items.meta: Sai Yud Market, town center · Open from ~06:00

items.name: Khanom Jeen Nam Ngiao Chiang Rai (behind the bus station)
items.blurb: A khanom jeen nam ngiao shop with a richer, bolder broth than the Shan version, sitting behind Mae Hong Son's bus station. People who like their nam ngiao strong and a touch spicy tend to come here; you can ask for extra. Prices are low and parking is easy thanks to the bus-station location.
items.meta: Behind Mae Hong Son bus station

items.name: Gung Khun Lung
items.blurb: A nice-looking spot near Su Tong Pae Bridge with an air-conditioned section up front and a café zone out back beside a clear stream where you can see the fish. They serve khanom jeen nam ngiao, and it's a good place to settle in over a meal followed by coffee and homemade ice cream — solid if you want both local food and a pretty view.
items.meta: Near Su Tong Pae Bridge · Streamside seating

items.name: Pa Wanna Khao Soi & Nam Ngiao
items.blurb: A shop doing both khao soi and nam ngiao in one place — handy if you're with a group and want to order one of each to share around. It draws steady reviews for a good hand in the kitchen and friendly prices.

items.name: Pa Jan Khao Soi
items.blurb: An old in-town khao soi shop that regulars drop by steadily. The broth is loaded with spice paste, and it's the pick for anyone who wants homey khao soi without a lot of fuss.

items.name: Nam Ngiao Secret Recipe Yam Mon
items.blurb: A nam ngiao shop that leans on its original nam ngiao chili and a special roasted chili, with bolder flavors than the usual Shan version. A good fit for anyone who likes a heavy hit of spice paste and the smell of roasted chili.

items.name: Janchai — Khanom Jeen Nam Ngiao & Khao Soi (Pai)
items.blurb: A shop on the Pai walking street doing both khanom jeen nam ngiao and khao soi. Handy if you're traveling around Pai and want local food without driving into Mae Hong Son town — easy to drop into while you wander the walking street.

items.name: Hot Khao Soi at Ban Rak Thai
items.blurb: Up at Ban Rak Thai village there's a shop serving piping-hot khao soi with crisp-outside, soft-inside fried tofu, set against tea plantations and a Yunnan-style lake. It's a meal that comes with both local food and a misty atmosphere — ideal if you're already driving up to Ban Rak Thai.
items.meta: Ban Rak Thai (Rak Thai) village · By the reservoir

blocks.title: How to make the most of it
blocks.html: Pa Nuan and the Sai Yud Market stall sell fast and often run out before afternoon, so if you're set on the famous spots, going between morning and noon is the safer bet. Bring cash too — most local shops still don't all take bank transfers.

blocks.text: How to make khao soi and nam ngiao taste even better

items: Squeeze in lime and add pickled greens — the khao soi here runs sweet and mellow, so a little sourness cuts through the coconut richness nicely.
Mix the crispy noodles all the way through — both khao soi and nam ngiao come topped with fried noodles; stir them in and eat while they're still crisp for the full texture.
Order fried sides to go with it — fried tofu or khang pong dipped in roasted dried chili is the combo locals eat all the time.
Try both styles — if you have time, have the Shan-style khao soi at Pa Nuan, then try the richer nam ngiao behind the bus station to clearly taste the difference.

blocks.text: Planning a full day along the noodle trail

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Eat your way through Mae Hong Son town

items.activity: Start the morning at Sai Yud Market
items.note: Have Shan-style khanom jeen nam ngiao with warm tofu while you browse the fresh local produce.
Order the chicken khao soi or the stir-fried khao soi — go before noon so it doesn't sell out.

items.activity: Sit streamside at Gung Khun Lung
items.note: Follow up with coffee and homemade ice cream, an easy break before dinner.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Head out to Pai for local bites

items.note: The road is winding — allow extra time and stop at the viewpoints along the way.

items.activity: Khanom jeen nam ngiao & khao soi at Janchai
items.note: It's right by the Pai walking street, so you can eat local without hunting around.
Keep grazing on Shan food and local sweets into the evening.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Up to Ban Rak Thai for khao soi in the mist

items.activity: Drive up to Ban Rak Thai
items.note: The climb is steep — drive carefully; mornings often have lovely mist.

items.activity: Hot khao soi by the reservoir
items.note: Have it with fried tofu and a view of the Yunnan tea plantations.
Follow up with Yunnan Chinese dishes like Yunnan pork knuckle and thousand-year pork if you still have room.

faq.q: How is Mae Hong Son khao soi different from Chiang Mai khao soi?
faq.a: Mae Hong Son khao soi carries a Shan influence — the coconut-curry broth comes out mellow and balanced and isn't as fiery as Chiang Mai's, so it's easy going even if you're not big on spice. The shop locals call a legend is Pa Nuan, open for over 60 years.

faq.q: Is Mae Hong Son nam ngiao spicy?
faq.a: The Shan-style nam ngiao in Mae Hong Son is a clear, pale-orange broth from tomatoes and kapok flowers, and it's milder than Chiang Rai nam ngiao. If you want it strong and bold, head to the Chiang Rai-style khanom jeen nam ngiao shop behind the bus station instead.

faq.q: What time should I go to eat at Pa Nuan?
faq.a: The shop is open 08:00–16:30 daily, but because it sells well and often runs out before afternoon, go between morning and noon to catch the full menu — and bring cash.

faq.q: Where can I get khao soi and nam ngiao without going into town?
faq.a: If you're traveling around Pai, drop by Janchai near the Pai walking street, which does both khao soi and khanom jeen nam ngiao. And if you head up to Ban Rak Thai, there's a shop serving hot khao soi with fried tofu and a Yunnan view.

faq.q: Roughly how much do khao soi and nam ngiao cost in Mae Hong Son?
faq.a: At most local shops khao soi runs about 40–60 THB a bowl, and khanom jeen nam ngiao about 30–45 THB a plate — easy on the wallet. Spots in tourist areas like Ban Rak Thai may run a little higher since you're paying for the view too.
